# Kulāvakajātaka (Ja 31)

**ID:** Ja 31
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Nestling Birds

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kulāvakajātaka* (Ja 31), translated as *The Nestling Birds*, belongs to the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. The framing narrative states that the Buddha delivered this tale while residing at Jetavana concerning a monk who drank water without straining it, opening with the verse line "Let the nestlings" [Readings from the Jatakas; SuttaCentral]. The core story describes a past birth of the Bodhisatta as the virtuous and public-spirited citizen Magha in a Magadha village; his deeds of communal welfare led to his rebirth as Sakka, king of the devas in Tāvatiṃsa heaven, alongside his fellow villagers [Mrs. Rhys Davids 1917; Murphy, Buddhist Boundary Markers]. In his household were four women: Goodness, Thoughtful, Joy, and Highborn [Murphy, Buddhist Boundary Markers]. While the first three performed meritorious acts and were consequently reborn as celestial companions or handmaidens of Sakka, Highborn performed no acts of goodwill and was reborn as a lowly crane [Hazra 1994; Murphy, Buddhist Boundary Markers]. Narrative scenes illustrating this story—depicting Sakka seated in *lalitāsana* on his mount Airāvata flanked by handmaidens—have been identified on eighth- to ninth-century Dvaravati Buddhist boundary stones (*sīmā*) at Muang Fa Daed in northeastern Thailand [Murphy, Buddhist Boundary Markers].

SuttaCentral records three full parallels to the text: the *Kulāvakasutta* of the Pali Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 11.6) and two Chinese Saṃyuktāgama versions, SA2 49 and SA 1222 (both titled 鳥巢) [SuttaCentral]. In his study of these parallel traditions, Marcus Bingenheimer notes the commentarial identification in the *Kulāvaka Jātaka* where the nestling birds (*kulāvakā*) are glossed as mythical *supaṇṇa* (*suparṇa*) fledglings inhabiting the lower ranges of Mount Sumeru [Bingenheimer, Studies in Agama Literature]. DharmaNexus identifies no significant automated text-reuse matches with a score of 10 or higher for this text [DharmaNexus].
